articles.title_orig: Three years after Oct. 7, Israeli strikes in Gaza grind on and deaths climb
articles.title_zh: Three years after Oct. 7, Israeli strikes in Gaza grind on and deaths climb
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lays a wreath during a state memorial ceremony in memory of those killed in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel, at Mount Herzl cemetery in Jerusalem on Oct. 5. Debbie Hill/Pool UPI via AP hide caption
TEL AVIV, Israel — As Israel marks three years since Hamas launched its surprise Oct. 7 attacks, Israelis are reeling from new revelations in Israeli and U.S. media that the country had been repeatedly warned by its regional allies that Hamas was planning to attack.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was personally warned about a potential Hamas attack, and his security agencies were notified repeatedly, in the weeks and days leading up to Oct. 7, 2023, four people in the Middle East with direct knowledge of the warnings told NPR.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz , The New York Times and The Atlantic first reported about the warnings.
Netanyahu has denied he was warned, calling the reports "fake news" and filing a defamation lawsuit last week against Israeli news outlets that published them. He and his defense minister have issued new warnings that Hamas could try to attack or "challenge" Israel on this Oct. 7 memorial day and leading up to national elections later this month.
But the Oct. 7, 2023, security failure — as well as Netanyahu's repeated refusal to take responsibility for it — has become a lightning rod in Israel as the prime minister seeks a new term in national elections this month.
"You didn't protect my son," yelled out one bereaved Israeli father whose son was killed in the Hamas-led attack, as the prime minister spoke at a memorial ceremony this week for the victims.
One warning came directly from the leader of Hamas in Gaza weeks before Oct. 7, a Palestinian mediator told NPR and other media outlets.
Former Palestinian Authority official Sufian Abu Zaida said he helped mediate secret Hamas-Israel talks for more than a year leading up to Oct. 7. He said Hamas wanted Israel to release Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and offered in exchange to release two living Israeli hostages and the bodies of two Israeli soldiers held in Gaza for years. But he said Israel was unwilling to release as many prisoners as Hamas had demanded.
On Sept. 14, 2023, Abu Zaida said, Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar dictated a message for him to deliver to Israel: "By the end of September, we will put cards on the table. There will be an earthquake in the negotiations, and the Israelis should prepare to empty their prisons."
He did not know what kind of earthquake Sinwar meant, but he said he sent the message to an Israeli intelligence official who acknowledged receiving it and to Mohammed Dahlan, a Palestinian confidant of the leader of the United Arab Emirates.
"What happened [on] the 7th of October is needless," Abu Zaida told NPR.
Days before the Oct. 7 attacks, the leader of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, called Netanyahu and told him that Hamas' leader in Gaza was planning a big assault against Israel, according to a person close to Dahlan. Dahlan was the Palestinian Authority's head of security in Gaza before Hamas seized control of the territory in 2007.
The Emirati leader told Netanyahu in a phone call that lasted more than 40 minutes that a "quake" would hit the region if no progress was achieved regarding a prisoner deal between Hamas and Israel, the person said.
The person spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity because of the diplomatic sensitivity of the call. The phone call was previously reported by Haaretz and The New York Times .
The UAE did not deny the report, saying only that it maintained dialogue with Israel.
People visit a memorial at a police station attacked by Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023, three years prior, in Sderot, southern Israel, on Oct. 4. Oded Balilty/AP hide caption
A senior Egyptian official told NPR that Egypt had specific intelligence about Hamas movements and that Egypt's head of intelligence at the time, Abbas Kamel, had traveled to Israel with two other senior officials and met with Israel's Mossad and Shin Bet intelligence chiefs.
The official said Kamel relayed a warning that Gaza was on the verge of an "explosion" because of Israel's blockade, the condition of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and concerns that Israel might move to annex the occupied West Bank.
The official was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. The Atlantic reported that Kamel's visit to Israel was on Sept 26.
Nimrod Novik, a fellow at the Israel Policy Forum think tank and a former top adviser to late Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres, told NPR that he was informed before Oct. 7 by a person with firsthand knowledge that Egypt had delivered warnings to several senior Israeli officials that "Gaza is about to explode in your face."
Novik said one warning was an "urgent and dramatic message" from Egypt, delivered to a person close to Netanyahu some 10 days prior to Oct. 7.
"I'm certain that the issue of the early warnings on October 7 is going to continue to play with heightened emotions as we approach Election Day," said Novik. "This is going to be an indictment for history, not just for the elections."
Netanyahu has blamed Israeli security organizations for failing to stop the Oct. 7 attacks. He and his government have yet to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the failures around Oct. 7, despite public demand.
The new reports about warnings issued to Israel "actually turn the story on its head," pointing the finger right back at the prime minister, said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
"It violates the basic narrative that Netanyahu tries to tell Israelis," said Talshir.

articles.title_zh: World's largest penguin colony hit by 'alarming' decline in numbers
articles.content_orig:
Almost two-thirds of the population of chinstrap penguins have disappeared from a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, aerial surveys suggest.
Zavodovski Island was home to the largest penguin colony in the world, but researchers who carried out the surveys say it has now lost that accolade.
According to the study, there were 63% fewer occupied nests of chinstrap penguins in 2025 than at the same time in 2011.
The research team say climate change is affecting the birds' food supply and survival, and the penguins may now be officially endangered.
Another species of penguin, the macaroni, also nests on the island and is thriving, which scientists believe is linked to their more varied diet.
Zavodovski is part of the South Sandwich Islands, a remote archipelago north of the Antarctic continent which is a UK overseas territory.
In 2011, it was hailed by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as home to the largest penguin colony in the world - with an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nesting on its bleak, rocky terrain.
BAS, which led this new research, says it is "one of the most extreme places in the world to undertake fieldwork".
A BAS team sailed for 15 days to reach the island and study its avian inhabitants, using drones, aerial photography and fitting tracking devices to 20 birds.
This research and satellite imagery suggested that - between 2011 and 2025 - the number of occupied chinstrap penguin nests declined by 63%.
The researchers say the "alarming" fall in the chinstrap population is all about the food supply and rising ocean temperatures brought about by climate change.
Prof Norman Ratcliffe, who led the research, explained that the chinstraps' "specialist diet" and preference for cooler waters appears to have left them vulnerable.
"With waters warming, the krill [that the chinstrap penguins eat] have moved southwards.
"Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food," he said.
The team examined other possible threats to the penguins' precarious existence on their remote island. Birds here nest in the shadow of an active volcano - Mount Curry, also aptly known as Mount Asphyxsia.
Sites downwind of the volcano have been given names including Stench Point, Noxious Bluff and Asphyxia Plain, because of the smell of fumes emitted from the crater.
Dr Ratcliffe told BBC News: "When you add all the penguin guano on top of that, and you really do have one of the smelliest places in the world.
"It's like a penguin Mordor."
Mount Curry's last major eruption was back in 2016, but the penguin declines that this study analysed have been steady and ongoing since 2011, suggesting that something else was happening.
Another concern was competition for the krill that chinstrap penguins rely on - possibly from migrating humpback whales. But, while the humpbacks eat huge quantities of krill, they also help boost krill production by fertilising marine plants that the krill feed on (with their huge quantities of whale poo).
Researchers say a more fundamental, climate-driven shift in ocean food supplies is to blame.
There is an unexpected element of this story that also adds to the picture of how - and why - this region is changing: While the chinstrap population has been declining, the number of macaroni penguins on the island has increased dramatically.
Macaroni penguins, scientists say, are more adaptable, because they have a broader, more flexible diet.
Tracking data from the study showed that the macaronis foraged in warmer waters to the northeast of the island, where scientists say they were were likely to be supplementing their diets with fish and other crustaceans.
Dr Ratcliffe said this shift was "biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica".
"Our data shows that the cold-adapted Antarctic chinstrap species are no longer thriving beside their sub-Antarctic neighbours," he added.
"It is further evidence of how rapid warming in the Antarctic is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems."
As for the title of world's largest penguin colony, scientists say that is now held by a site more than 5,000km away - on the other side of the Antarctic continent - Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
The research is published in the journal Current Biology .

Three years ago today, Israel and her people endured the most horrific acts of terror in the nation’s modern history on October 7, 2023. The Holy Land held its National Day of Remembrance earlier this week, but Jews and Christians in the U.S. and around the world are taking today to remember the more than 1,200 victims, the 251 people who were kidnapped, and the countless lives and communities that continue to be affected.
JNS reports that Israel’s envoy to the Christian world George Deek praised the Flags of Fellowship movement ahead of the annual Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit.
Three years after October 7, to see millions of Christians around the world publicly raise Israel’s flag is a powerful reminder that friendship can speak louder than hatred. More than 5.2 million Israeli flags, over 4,375 churches, universities and organizations, in 14 countries. WOW.
At a time when Israel and the Jewish people have faced extraordinary hatred, millions of Christians are choosing something different: friendship, remembrance and solidarity. I am deeply grateful to the International Fellowship of Christians and Jews, to Yael Eckstein, and to every pastor, church and community taking part in this remarkable initiative.
To our Christian friends around the world: thank you for standing with Israel. We see you. We appreciate you. And we will never take your friendship for granted.

More than 1,000 Christian leaders and influencers from 117 countries arrived in Israel on Monday for the second consecutive year of the summit. Around 300 of the participants are between the ages of 18 and 29. Summit founder Mike Evans says he hopes young Christians will see Israel for themselves and hear directly from those affected by October 7.
Much like Flags of Fellowship, the Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit carries the powerful message that Israel does not stand alone, building connections based on truth, courage, and a determination to confront anti-Semitism.
The Fellowship and our supporters pray for the families and remember the victims of October 7 alongside the 4,375 churches and synagogues around the world participating in Flags of Fellowship and the Christian ambassadors who have just arrived in Israel.

articles.title_orig: Rising seas threaten the world’s migratory shorebirds
articles.title_zh: Rising seas threaten the world’s migratory shorebirds
articles.content_orig:
Birds undertake some of the world’s most impressive migrations , travelling hundreds to thousands of kilometres every year in search of safe breeding grounds and seasonally abundant food resources. For many birds, migration is the key to their success . However, migration can also make species more vulnerable to threats.
Shorebirds — species that include sandpipers, plovers and oystercatchers — live and migrate along the world’s coastlines. Over the last several decades, coastal development has led to the loss of shorebird habitats in many areas of the world, driving population declines in multiple species . Now, a new threat is emerging: climate change-driven sea-level rise.
But how exactly does sea-level rise impact shorebirds, and just how serious is this threat?
Our new study reviews the evidence from 37 published papers to provide the first comprehensive overview of the threat of sea-level rise to the world’s shorebirds. Long story short: things aren’t looking good.
Shorebirds — as their name suggests — live along the shore, relying primarily on coastal ecosystems like  beaches, salt marshes and tidal flats. As sea levels rise, these vital habitats shrink.
Some coastal ecosystems may persist in the face of sea-level rise by moving inland with the rising waters, but this isn’t always possible. More than half of the world’s largest cities are within 100 kilometres of a coast , meaning that the presence of coastal infrastructure often blocks these pathways.
This leads to a phenomenon known as coastal squeeze — where ecosystems are increasingly squeezed between the rising waters and an inland barrier (such as dikes and seawalls built to protect homes and businesses), leading to decreases in habitat.
Loss of habitat has obvious implications for migratory shorebirds: less access to food, less space for nesting and more competition with other individuals.
But habitat loss isn’t the only threat to these species. Sea-level rise may also impact shorebirds in different ways, leading to changes in prey distribution , reproductive success , feeding time and many other factors.
Among the 37 studies that we examined, 21 predicted negative impacts of sea-level rise on shorebird habitats such as declines in habitat area or quality, while 17 predicted negative impacts on shorebird populations or individuals such as decreased survival or abundance.
Sea-level rise is expected to drive substantial habitat loss at many sites of international importance for migratory shorebirds. These include San Francisco Bay and Humboldt Bay in the United States, the Colorado River Delta and Marismas Nacionales in Mexico and the Yellow Sea region in East Asia, each of which supports 150,000 to more than one million shorebirds annually.
Habitat loss at these kinds of migratory bottleneck sites where large numbers of shorebirds congregate over a short period of time may hit populations particularly hard. Because so many birds funnel through these sites during migration, habitat loss in these areas may impact multiple species and entire populations. This means these sites must be a priority for conservation.
Maintaining coastal ecosystems and protecting them from the threat of sea-level rise will be essential for the survival of thriving shorebird populations. But coastal ecosystems aren’t only important for shorebirds. They also support thousands of other species and provide valuable ecosystem services such as coastal protection, water filtration and carbon storage.
In order to preserve these habitats and the species that depend on them, governments will need to make a serious effort to mitigate the impacts of coastal squeeze. Rather than continuing to armour our shorelines, decision makers should prioritize solutions that will protect human communities while also benefitting coastal ecosystems .
The shape that these actions take may vary from place to place. In some areas, it may be necessary to relocate coastal infrastructure to give ecosystems space to move inland as sea levels rise — an approach referred to as “managed retreat.” In other areas, scientists and practitioners are looking at how we can use sediment recovered from dredging to enhance or create new habitats.
However we choose to respond to sea-level rise, urgent action will be required to preserve shorebirds and their fascinating migrations for generations to come.

articles.title_orig: WHO endorses lifestyle changes over GLP-1 drugs in child obesity fight
articles.title_zh: WHO endorses lifestyle changes over GLP-1 drugs in child obesity fight
articles.content_orig:
Children under 10 should not be given obesity drugs or GLP-1 weight-loss injections such as Mounjaro and Wegovy, new global guidelines from the World Health Organization say.
Most of these medications are only licensed for children or adolescents older than this, but some doctors prescribe them off-label, and drug companies are testing them in children as young as six.
WHO says the care should focus on healthy eating and exercise, not medicine or surgery, although they do not oppose drug trials.
Some digital technology, such as activity trackers and any online games that encourage the player to be more active and move, might be useful, it says, based on the limited evidence available.
Estimates suggest 170 million children and adolescents worldwide are obese.
That includes 70 million children aged 5–9. Obesity prevalence in this age group has quadrupled since 1990, rising from 2% to 8%.
In 2024, 35 million children under the age of five were overweight.
Obesity increases the risk of many different diseases, including type 2 diabetes.
Dr Luz De Rigil, Director of Nutrition and Food Safety at WHO, said: "For children under 10, WHO does not recommend obesity medicines, bariatric surgery or weight-management devices. This is a strong recommendation."
These might be appropriate for older children and adolescents when lifestyle approaches have failed and if the individual is "mentally and physically prepared" for the treatment, she added.
She said WHO recognises this is an evolving field and will continue to evaluate the evidence.
WHO's head of Nutrition and Food Safety Actions, Laurence Grummer-Strawn, said: "We are particularly concerned in this age group, if you are starting children very early on to using a GLP-1 or drugs like this, when does that stop?
"We don't really have evidence that you can use this as a temporary treatment and then turn to something dietary later on in life.
"We are very cautious about jumping in without clear evidence," he said.

The barriers to entry for game creation are rapidly diminishing as AI makes game development more accessible to people without traditional programming, design, or illustration skills. The latest example is an experiment from Google Labs.
On Wednesday, the tech giant’s public incubator and experimental platform launched a new AI-powered game-creation platform called Playground, which allows users to build browser-based games using simple text prompts, eliminating the need for coding expertise.
With Playground, creators can select a genre, such as trivia or racing, or start a project from scratch. They can specify whether they want a 2D or 3D game and choose between single-player and multiplayer experiences before describing the desired mechanics, gameplay, and visual style. Playground also allows users to upload visuals that its AI can transform into game assets tailored to the game’s overall art style.
Once created, games can be played on both mobile devices and computers. Projects can remain private, be shared through a link, or be published to Playground’s Explore gallery. Published games can support features such as leaderboards, while creators can continue modifying their projects even after they have been released.
Google also indicated that it plans to add Unity Spark integration in a future update. The integration could give Playground users access to additional 3D capabilities and “professional-level” game mechanics through Unity’s technology, further expanding what can be created through the platform.
Playground is initially available to users aged 18 and older in the U.S., with Google planning to expand availability to additional countries. Browsing and playing games in the catalog is free, while game generation relies on a weekly token system. The free tier provides a limited number of tokens, while Google One AI subscribers receive higher usage limits.
Google’s launch places Playground within a growing market of AI-assisted game-development tools. Roblox, for example, announced its own Build feature in July, enabling users to create games through natural-language prompts.
The initiative also builds on Google’s broader interest in gaming. The company previously explored cloud gaming through Stadia back in 2022, and later on continued incorporating games into other platforms, including YouTube Playables , a dedicated hub offering a selection of instantly playable web-based games.

articles.title_orig: World leaders solemnly mark 3 years since Oct. 7, as Hamas and Iran celebrate anniversary
articles.title_zh: World leaders solemnly mark 3 years since Oct. 7, as Hamas and Iran celebrate anniversary
articles.content_orig:
The Nova music festival memorial site on Oct. 07, 2026.
The world changed when Hamas attacked Israelis on Oct. 7, 2023 , catalyzing devastating conflict throughout the region . But within Israel, political sentiments have changed surprisingly little.
To some, the attack fulfilled long-term right-wing warnings that Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza would yield disaster; and the attack was incontrovertible proof that Palestinians will never live in peace with Israel.
Israeli left-wingers, for their part, have long held that a festering military rule over Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, and failure to reach peace, would inevitably lead to violent conflagration. For them, Oct. 7 only proved that they had been right all along.
The standoff raises crucial questions. In three years since Oct. 7, how has the attack changed Israeli society? And how will the answer affect upcoming elections in Israel?
To be sure, there have been cataclysmic changes in Israel, and the Middle East at large, since Oct. 7. The war in Gaza that began that day has become Israel’s longest war. A relatively stable ceasefire with Lebanon from 2006 to 2023 ended when Hezbollah, a Shi’a militia group, fired on Israel the day after Hamas’ attack; after multiple escalations since then, the current ceasefire is precarious. Israel and the U.S. have waged two full-blown wars with Iran, and the Middle East is still threatened by spin-off conflicts.
The losses Israelis suffered on Oct. 7 and since then have affected the country collectively and profoundly. For two years, many Israelis went from demonstration to demonstration demanding that their government prioritize a deal with Hamas to release Israeli hostages. Hundreds of thousands have spent the last three years in and out of active reserve duty.
Since 2023, Israel has seen record levels of emigration and growing international isolation. Sixty-one percent of Israelis told pollsters for the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) that the national mood is poor .
Moreover, the destruction of Palestinian life and society , still ongoing , will one day force a terrible reckoning within Israel.
What’s less visible, and more surprising, is what has stayed the same. Israelis’ attitudes towards Palestinians, occupation, and conflict have become more extreme. But I would argue that Israeli public opinion today says much more about how Israel had changed prior to Oct. 7. The change in national attitudes since that fateful day has been moderate and consistent with what came before.
In December 2022, almost a year before Oct. 7, support for peace through a two-state solution hit a historic low. In the joint Palestinian-Israeli survey I conduct together with colleagues at Tel Aviv University and the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, support stood at 39% of Israelis that year—the lowest since the 1990s. Among Jewish respondents, just 34% supported a two-state solution, and 37% believed Israel should permanently annex the West Bank while Palestinians would have limited rights.
When we conducted the study again in mid-2024, Jews were twice as likely to support a single, Israeli-dominated unequal state as they were to support two states.
Palestinian attitudes in 2022 were similar. Just one-third supported two states. Both sides showed a mirror-image majority who distrusted the other. In surveys by the IDI from that same time, 59% of Jewish Israelis defined themselves as right-wing; just 12% said they were left-wing.
What changed after Oct. 7? This July, the Tel Aviv University Peace Index survey found that support for two states stood at 31%, an eight-point decline in the four years since 2022. Now, IDI surveys find that just over 60% of Israeli Jews describe themselves as right-wing, just a few points higher than late 2022.
Israel has changed, but this change began years before Oct. 7 2023. In 2010 , no fewer than 71% of Israelis supported a two-state solution in the joint surveys. The years that followed were plagued by stagnation and dissipation of any peace process, regular wars with Hamas, and a heavily nationalist government in Israel. It stands to reason that these phenomena pushed Israeli society further to the right. Support for the two-state solution eroded slowly, then rapidly by the end of the decade.
That shift was self-reinforcing: the more right-wing Israelis became (primarily the Jewish population), the more elected leaders took ever-more radical positions such as supporting settlement expansion and de facto annexation in the West Bank. In 2019, Prime Minister Netanyahu began referring to extending sovereignty over parts of the West Bank, or de jure annexation . The current government accelerated those processes drastically.
Study after study shows that Arab citizens of Israel have remained the strongest supporters of peace, before and after the current wars. But with Jewish Israeli and Palestinian attitudes so dismal in the years before Oct. 7, the chances of resurgent violence almost seemed inevitable.
In other words, most Israelis did not radically transform their worldview after Oct. 7. In fact, hardline political trends were among the many factors contributing to the terrible escalation to begin with.
Another thing that hasn’t changed in Israel during the last three years of war: hopes for peace. The number of Israeli Jews who self-describe as left-wing has barely shifted. In a May survey for the Institute for National Security Studies, about 20% of the total population, Jews and Arabs, define themselves as left-wing, and a similar share typically say they are centrist. These groups embrace a commitment to democracy, liberal values, separation of religion and state, and reject the religious fundamentalism of the current government.
The left remains committed to peace via diplomacy and Palestinian self-determination. In a mid-2025 survey I conducted for a peace organization called A Land for All, where I am also an active member, the large majority of self-defined left-wing Israelis, and nearly half of centrists, supported a basic two-state solution.
Do peace attitudes even matter, when there is no peace process? That may be theoretical for now, but elections aren’t. Israelis will be voting on Oct. 27. Polls show the voters deeply divided , just as they were in the elections held between 2019 and 2022.
Netanyahu’s far-right coalition is not doing well. Nearly all polls show his coalition parties well below their actual result in 2022. And most mainstream polls show a consistent majority for today’s opposition parties.
At first glance, these shifts might seem antithetical. Aren’t these ideological and electoral trends moving in contradictory directions: more right-wing, but a majority against the current government?
It turns out that even the Israeli electoral contradiction is not new. During the five elections from 2019 through 2022, a majority of Israelis were right-wing and voted for right-wing parties. But to form a coalition, some of those parties no longer supported Netanyahu and refused to join a coalition under his leadership. Netanyahu therefore commanded only about half the seats in parliament following four of these cycles. Neither side had a clear or firm coalition majority, and the country was thrown into electoral turmoil five times over.
But if all mainstream polls show the anti-Netanyahu parties winning, including right-wing opposition parties, shouldn’t that mean a decisive outcome against him this time? Not quite: no poll shows Israel’s Jewish, Zionist parties reaching a majority in October.
And in Israel’s right-wing, populist discourse, the main opposition party leaders opposed to Netanyahu now, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman, with similar statements from frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot , insist that parties representing Arab citizens must not be part of a coalition after Oct. 7. Two seaside resorts in New England are among the best on the planet, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
The travel publication released a list of the 50 best resorts in the world on Tuesday, part of its 39th Annual Readers’ Choice Awards , and Chatham Bars Inn in Chatham ranked No. 18. Weekapaug Inn in Westerly, R.I. ranked No. 28.
Chatham Bars Inn , which was also named the No. 1 resort in New England , is “a benchmark of luxury on the Cape,” Conde Nast Traveler wrote.
“If you’re looking for a full-service resort with all the bells and whistles and then some, this is it, including an eight-acre private farm to stock the resort’s numerous dining and drinking outlets; one of the better spas on the Cape; an expansive pool deck with F&B service; a private quarter-mile beachfront; tennis courts with lessons available; and a 24-hour gym,” wrote the publication.
Resort officials celebrated on social media , writing, “Thank you to our incredible team and to our guests and supporters who voted for us. We’re grateful to be recognized alongside so many remarkable destinations.”
Weekapaug Inn, also named the No. 2 resort in New England , is a historic getaway in Rhode Island.
“A recently renovated legendary seaside inn on the National Register of Historic Places, the 27-room, six-suite Weekapaug Inn is a three-hour drive from New York and less than two from Boston—ideal for a quick weekend jaunt,” wrote Conde Nast Traveler .
Visitors enjoy guided nature walks, golf, tennis, and boating expeditions in historic vessels, noted the publication.
Officials at Weekapaug Inn also shared their excitement on social media , writing, “Thank you to the Condé Nast Traveler readers who voted, and to our incredible teams for truly delivering the best of service, cuisine, and luxury, year after year. articles.title_orig: What happened in the first Maine Senate debate between Collins and Jackson
articles.title_zh: What happened in the first Maine Senate debate between Collins and Jackson
articles.content_orig:
Republican challenged by Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Senate race says she opposes Iran war and Canada tariffs
Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine , pointedly distanced herself from Donald Trump in a televised debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, as she sought to present an image of independence in a state that has voted against Trump three times.
Proclaiming herself as not the US president’s “favorite senator”, Collins made the highly unusual boast for a Republican that she had voted with Joe Biden, a Democrat, more than 90% of the time when he was president. She also emphasized her differences with her fellow Republicans , saying she voted against her own party more than any other senator.
Collins’s defensiveness came amid a determined onslaught from Jackson, 58, a veteran former state legislator who was getting his first chance to present himself to a broad audience since replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic candidate in a contest that could be vital to the party’s hopes of winning the Senate.
Platner, a former harbor master, was forced to withdraw from the race in July after facing sexual assault allegations, which he denied, leaving Democrats racing against the clock to replace a candidate who had built up momentum campaigning on a populist progressive platform.
Jackson painted Collins as a Trump loyalist, saying she voted with the president 96% of the time. He also doggedly focused on her 2018 vote for the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, tying it to the court’s subsequent overturning of Roe v Wade, which had for half a century guaranteed the national right to abortion.
“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in a pithy opening statement. “Eight years ago today, Maine women went to DC and begged Senator Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but she did it anyways.
“He helped overturn Roe v Wade, and today she says she has no regrets. Would you trust her to pick the next supreme court justice?”
Collins, 73, who has been a senator since 1996, has frequently presented herself as a moderate who stands against more radical trends in her own party. The posture is in line with Maine’s profile as a more Democratic-leaning state, which Trump has not won in any of his three presidential campaigns and which has voted for Democratic presidential candidates in every election since 1992.
Nevertheless, Collins went to unusual lengths to differentiate herself from Trump on a range of issues, including the war with Iran, which she said she voted to end nine times, calling it “not well thought out”.
Collins reacted with something close to alarm when the moderator, Gregg Lagerquist, said Trump had suggested that the president might pay a campaign visit to Maine.
after newsletter promotion
“I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” she said. “He’s talking about going to a lot of different states. I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator.”
Collins stressed her differences with the president on specific issues pertinent to the Maine economy, including rural healthcare and tariffs against Canada, with which the state shares a border.
“I have been the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada,” she said. “Canada is not China. It’s our neighbor and our friends.”
Polls show the two candidates running neck and neck.

articles.title_orig: US 30-year mortgage rate hits highest in nearly three years
articles.title_zh: US 30-year mortgage rate hits highest in nearly three years
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home more challenging at a time when housing prices are already high. Nam Y. Huh/AP hide caption
Carrie Goldstein's dream for a new home started with a family reunion at her cousin's home in Milwaukee. The home was old with character and she could walk anywhere from the front door.
"We were kind of in awe and drooling over her walkability," Goldstein says.
It was the lifestyle Goldstein wanted but lacked in her Cleveland suburb, which she says is also pretty walkable – with one major issue.
"There are lots of sidewalks," she says. "But you can't really go anywhere."
She brainstormed with her husband and realized nearby Rocky River was where they wanted to live. It was still a suburb, but with a quaint downtown and the option to walk to Lake Erie.
But as much as she wanted to move, one thing stopped her cold. The mortgage she would have to pay. Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home impossible for many people at a time when housing prices are also sky high.
Goldstein is running into a problem that's affecting many households at a time when people have already been struggling with years of high inflation: The rising cost of borrowing.
Carrie Goldstein stands outside her home on October 4, 2026. Home prices and mortgage rates prevent her from moving. Mike Goldstein hide caption
Bond markets influence all types of borrowing costs across the economy – and as yields have surged to their highest in decades, they've pushed up all kinds of interest rates paid by consumers, from loans for homes to cars and higher education.
And those rates are likely to continue moving up after the Federal Reserve in September raised interest rates for the first time this year – while signaling an additional hike could come this year.
Rate hikes from the Federal Reserve filter through the economy and are meant to slow down consumer and business spending by making people hesitant to take out a more expensive loan to pay for a car or a home – both essential purchases for many people.
"If you need to borrow, boy, it's really not a good time," says John Diamond, senior director of the Center for Tax and Budget Policy at the Baker Institute.
Buying a home is a key example of how households are affected when borrowing costs rise in the economy.
While mortgage rates were falling at the start of this year, they reversed upward after the U.S. war with Iran spooked the bond market by raising worries about inflation. As a result, mortgage rates, which are influenced by the bond markets, have surged this year.
For example, at the current 7.28% level for the average 30-year fixed rate mortgage, a person could end up paying about $900 more a month compared with the 3% pandemic-era rates for a median priced home.
As expected, fewer homeowners are willing or capable of making that financial leap, even if they have long since outgrown their current home. Existing house sales in August were down about 1.2% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.
It's not just mortgage costs that are making Americans like Goldstein wince.
Alongside her dreams of owning a home in a walkable neighborhood, Goldstein is ready for a new car. Her old one is 11 years old, has 150,000 miles and plenty of quirks. The repair costs are approaching the point where they'll be more than the value of the actual car.
But a four-year loan for a used car is about three percentage points higher compared with the start of 2022, right around when auto loans began to shed their pandemic-era low rates and started climbing up.
"You can't go and get a car for $150 or $180 bucks anymore a month," she says about the car payments she would be facing.
Although so far the Fed has only delivered a modest quarter of a percentage point, it's adding to the higher borrowing costs at a time when households are already dealing with inflation and higher prices for other types of borrowing.
"It's added to higher mortgage payments. Higher student loan payments. Higher prices because of inflation," Diamond says. "That's what makes it really painful."
And that could mean that households could continue to delay any big purchases requiring a loan.
Goldstein is one of them. She says she can afford to wait on the car and house. But eventually she unsubscribed from real estate updates for that walkable suburb.
"It just became more and more disheartening when I did the math," Goldstein says. "It's just not in the cards."

articles.title_orig: A UMass study has revealed two of the world’s loudest birds. Here’s what they sound like.
articles.title_zh: A UMass study has revealed two of the world’s loudest birds. Here’s what they sound like.
articles.content_orig:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
University of Massachusetts Amherst biologists have discovered two contenders for the world’s loudest birds, both from Brazil.
The bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema are louder than jackhammers and may just be the loudest birds in the world, according to a study published in Evolution by UMass professor Jeff Podos and his former graduate student João Menezes.
This isn’t the first groundbreaking discovery for Podos. In fact, his research established a Guinness World Record in 2019 when he discovered that the Amazon’s white bellbird had the world’s loudest bird call, louder than a revving chainsaw.
The latest discovery is the result of Podos and Menezes’s years of ongoing research to understand the role evolutionary biology plays in how birds communicate with each other. Their research aims to solve the mystery of why some birds are so much louder than others, and whether there are certain physical traits that can predict their volume.
Menezes said it’s difficult to measure how loud a bird call is in the field, and there’s little data available. But using cutting-edge tools, Podos and Menezes have gathered reliable amplitude data on 123 species throughout Massachusetts and Brazil, 113 of which had never before had their volume catalogued.
“We’ve been able to vastly increase the number of species for which there is amplitude data,” Podos said. “This is basic, foundational research that no one else has managed to do on this scale, and it points to all sorts of other questions that would be fun to follow up.”
Podos and Menezes discovered there’s a 58-decibel range in the volume of bird calls, from the hummingbird, whose calls are 64 decibels and about the volume of a normal conversation, to bare-throated bellbirds and red-legged seriemas, who register at over 120 decibels.
They found that the loudest birds are typically bigger, with wider beak openings and bulky muscles that may allow greater air compression for explosive volume. But Podos and Menezes said there’s still a lot unknown about how birds communicate.
“We now know some of the hows,” Menezes said. “Bigger bodies and wider beaks. But we’ve yet to discover the whys, and we probably need much more data from many more species to be able to tease out what’s going on on the ecological and evolutionary front.”

articles.title_zh: Exclusive: Paxton privately blames campaign woes on Iran war, gas prices

Texas attorney general acknowledged affordability was his party’s ‘biggest problem’ heading into the midterms
US politics live – latest updates
Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general running as the Republican candidate in a competitive Senate race, admitted privately that rising fuel prices as a result of Donald Trump’s Iran war were hurting his party before the midterms in the latest leaked audio recording.
Asked what issues were “dragging” his campaign at a closed-door fundraising event, Paxton replied, “It’s not tariffs … it’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel,” according to an audio recording shared with Axios.
“When it’s over $6 per gallon for diesel … people are feeling the pinch,” Paxton said.
Paxton acknowledged affordability was Republicans’ “biggest problem” heading into next month’s election, citing polling numbers that indicate Democrats are ahead in many competitive races – including his own.
Trump has tried to change the narrative around affordability, insisting his administration has done more to lower everyday prices for Americans than Democrats. Trump, who picked Paxton to run as the Republican in the Texas Senate race, will join Paxton at a rally in San Antonio on Wednesday evening.
But Paxton appeared to recognize the uphill battle facing Republicans , telling people at the closed-door events that “so many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable”.
“I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t, you know, I don’t know what’s behind some of the decisions,” Paxton said.
The Guardian has asked Paxton’s campaign for comment.
Madison Cercy, a spokesperson for Paxton’s campaign, said in a statement that the Texas attorney general’s comments were “a non-story”.
“The attorneygeneral said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store,” Cercy said.
“President Trump is doing everything he can to bring prices down, and Ken Paxton is going to Washington to help him by putting money back in families’ pockets with a bigger child tax credit and larger deductions for health care and buying a home. Texans need immediate relief, and everyone knows James Talarico will raise your taxes,” Cercy added.
Recent polling from the Associated Press/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research indicates most adults blame Trump for poor economic conditions. Approximately 74% of Americans said the economy was leaning poorly. Another 65% of survey respondents said they blame Trump’s policies directly for higher costs.
In the audio recording, obtained by Axios, Paxton said he was trying to help lower costs in ways that he could, such as through his proposed tax cut plan that includes healthcare and housing write-offs.
after newsletter promotion
Axios’s reporting is just the latest leaked audio clip of Paxton being critical of his own party.
Earlier this week, Politico reported that Paxton privately admitted to people at a closed-door event that outside forces in Washington DC were controlling much of his campaign messaging.
“I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming – you know – from DC,” Paxton said, according to an audio recording obtained by Politico.
Last week, the New York Times reported that Paxton admitted that Trump’s Republican midterm convention “dropped” his polling numbers.
Paxton is locked in a competitive race with the progressive Democrat James Talarico . Polls show Paxton and Talarico are neck-and-neck, but Talarico has a small lead over the Texas attorney general.

articles.title_orig: Nobel Prize in chemistry awarded to Kagan and Soai for untangling mirror images in molecules
articles.title_zh: Nobel Prize in chemistry awarded to Kagan and Soai for untangling mirror images in molecules
articles.content_orig:
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for providing a solution to the chemical mystery of life's asymmetry.
The researchers discovered how nature exclusively makes the correct version of a molecule - rather than its mirror image.
For example, amino acid molecules, the building blocks of proteins, exist as two forms that are each other's mirror image.
But living organisms on Earth only function with one of those forms. The Nobel laureates answered the question: why does life favour just one of these mirror image molecules over the other.
In organic chemistry, this property is known as "chirality", so chiral molecules have both right and left-handed forms.
You can think of them as looking like our hands - not identical, but each a mirror image of the other.
And while nature almost exclusively produces the version it requires to function, chemical reactions in a lab usually create a 50-50 mix of both left- and right-handed molecules.
When it comes to making drugs, this is particularly significant, because each version behaves differently when it interacts with our bodies.
So, one might have disease-fighting properties, while the other version does nothing or even causes harm.
The development of the Thalidomide drug is an example of this. In the 1950s it was prescribed to pregnant women suffering with morning sickness. But it is a chiral molecule - the right-handed version is an effective treatment, but the left-hand is toxic.
The original drug given was a mixture of the two, and it was later discovered that the body will convert between the two. The result was thousands of children, born to women who took the drug, developed severe disabilities.
Speaking to the Nobel Prize press conference this morning over the phone, Kenso Soai said: "This is one of the most exciting days of my life."
By solving the mystery of chirality, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai worked out how to design chemical reactions to produce much more of the desired version of a molecule.
Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, explained: "Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality - the selective production of the correct version of a molecule - can emerge spontaneously.
"The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."
Henri Kagan, who is at Université Paris-Sud, first discovered a new way of manipulating chemical reactions in 1986. This allowed him to create a greater excess of one of the mirror images than had previously been thought possible.
Kenso Soai from Tokyo University of Science took the next step in 1995. He published a scientific paper in the journal Nature describing the first ever chemical reaction that had the potential to be homochiral - producing only the desired version of an organic molecule.
In 2003, he finally succeeded in controlling a reaction in which only one of the two possible mirror images was formed.
"Other than life itself," the Nobel Committee said in a statement, "no one had previously achieved this feat".
At the press conference on Wednesday, Kenso Soai praised the "many, many excellent researchers" in this field.
Professor Robert Mokaya, president of the UK's Royal Society of Chemistry said it was a "powerful example of how fundamental chemistry can underpin solutions to some of the biggest challenges facing society".
"Different isomers (or versions of molecules) can have completely different biological and physical effects, so they are crucial in finding effective medicines to treat all sorts of illnesses," he added.
Prof Angus Davison, from the University of Nottingham, studies the biology of chirality and said that the Nobel-winning chemistry could help reveal how and why life favours "one-handedness".
"In ways that we don't yet quite understand, the chirality of the basic building blocks of life ends up making bodies that are themselves also chiral," he told BBC News.
This was the foundation, he explained, of our hearts being on left hand side of our bodies and snail shells that coil to the right.
Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said the research awarded this year's prize has become part of "our basic understanding of how chemistry functions".
He said showing how a mirror image is created is "probably the most fundamental question in life - because somehow that happened four billion years ago when life was created. And now we have, for the first time, mimicked that in the lab".

The Atlantic hurricane season has been eerily quiet—tropical storm Isaias could change that
Tropical storm Isaias is expected to become a hurricane by Thursday, meteorologists say
By Jackie Flynn Mogensen edited by Claire Cameron
Join Our Community of Science Lovers!
Tropical Storm Isaias, a cyclone in the Gulf of Mexico, is expected to strengthen into a hurricane by Thursday, according to the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). If it does, Isaias would be the latest forming first Atlantic hurricane on record.
As of Wednesday morning, Isaias sat about 260 miles (420 kilometers) off the coast of Progreso, Mexico, and is headed toward the U.S. Gulf Coast, including parts of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida, NOAA forecasts .
Isaias’ winds are up to some 45 miles per hour (75 kilometers per hour) as of this writing. To be considered a hurricane, winds must hit or surpass 74 mph (119 kmh).

If Isaias makes landfall as expected, the storm will likely bring strong gusts and heavy rainfall, with the potential for flash flooding and dangerous storm surge, says Jennifer Tate, a meteorologist at NOAA's Weather Prediction Center.
As Scientific American previously reported , hurricane activity in the Atlantic typically begins in June and peaks in September. But this year, the region has been quiet—with no hurricanes all season. Soon-to-be Hurricane Isaias would mark a historically late arrival for the first hurricane of the season.
The quiet is in part due to El Niño , meteorologists say. In an El Niño year, waters in the Pacific are unusually warm. This can drive global weather patterns, including in the Atlantic Ocean. There, high vertical wind shear—changes in wind speed or direction with altitude—typically make it difficult for hurricanes to form during El Niño years.
“It is common during El Niño patterns for the Atlantic to be quieter in terms of hurricanes,” Tate says, “whereas the Eastern Pacific and the Pacific in general, is more active. And we have seen that this year.”
Indeed, in the Pacific, hurricanes have threatened Hawaii to an unusually high degree this season.
For those on the Gulf Coast, Tate recommends staying up to date on hurricane forecasts , getting prepared with food and supplies in the case of a power outage, and following any local evacuation orders.

The World Climbing Europe Series 2026 concluded in Leipzig, Germany, with closely contested Speed finals. Spain and Ukraine each claimed two medals.
Ukraine’s Daria Tkachova won gold in 7.88 seconds, finishing ahead of Poland’s Magdalena Blachnicka, who stopped the clock at 8.58. The victory adds to Tkachova’s bronze medal from St. Pölten, Austria, earlier this year.

Ukraine’s Mariia Shymkova, who won silver in Žilina, returned to the podium in third place. She clocked 7.58 to narrowly beat teammate Sofiia Tulchynska’s 7.63.

articles.title_orig: 11 Places to See the World's Most Magnificent Wildlife Migrations
articles.title_zh: 11 Places to See the World's Most Magnificent Wildlife Migrations
articles.content_orig:
Seeing an immense number  of creatures assembled in one place is a phenomenon worth travelling for. Here’s when, where and how to experience some of nature’s wildest gatherings.
Seeing any animal in the wild is a privilege — but seeing huge numbers is something else. For a start, it’s both humbling and heartening to encounter any species in abundance. It’s also genuinely exciting. When big groups of creatures seasonally cluster in one place, there’s always something to watch — from courting and mating to fighting or family-raising. It may be a sensory assault, too: noise, tumult, pungent smells, crashing waters, mad flurries of dust. And where masses gather to move together, hungry predators may lurk, adding a macabre but fascinating dimension. Here, we’ve picked the most dramatic migrations through the year and around the globe.
When to go: December to March
How does an insect the weight of a paperclip make a journey of 3,000 miles? That’s the feat of the extraordinary monarch butterfly, which somehow flutters from its summer breeding grounds — spread across Canada and the American northeast — to a patch of oyamel fir forest in the highlands west of Mexico City. Most only survive for a month or so but, in autumn, a generation emerges that lives eight times as long, capable of making this perilous trip. How they know where to go is a mystery — the butterflies that migrate are the great-great-grandchildren of those that left Mexico the previous spring. No matter, the results are spectacular: millions upon millions of orange-black wings blanketing trees, raining like tickertape. The Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, in the mountains of Michoacán state, is home to more than half of the overwintering colonies of the monarch butterfly’s eastern population. The sanctuary of El Rosario is easiest to reach; lesser-visited Sierra Chincua can be explored on horseback. The colourful, cobblestoned Mineral de Angangueo makes a good base.
The Indigenous Sámi of Europe’s far north work to their own calendar. Their year has eight seasons, and giđđa (spring) means melting snows, fast-increasing daylight and reindeer on the move: around April, the animals start migrating from their inland pastures towards the coast for summer grazing. Norway has around 275,000 reindeer, some wild, but mostly semi-domesticated herds that are ushered across the country’s Arctic plateaus by Sámi families whose livelihoods have depended on the practice for generations. Finnmarksvidda, an empty vastness of low hills, glacial lakes, pine barrens, birch woods and bogs in northernmost Norway, is a Sámi stronghold, where a few operators offer the chance to join the herders on the move. Days are shaped by the reindeer and the weather, perhaps involving sledding, snowmobiling or feeding the animals, followed by sharing stories around the fire, feasting on Arctic fish and sleeping in lavvus (traditional tents). Seeing swathes of animals trot across the tundra is a treat; being immersed in Sámi culture is an even greater privilege.
A strange thing happens off the South African coast each winter in the Southern Hemisphere: sardines in their millions, maybe billions, swarm north from Cape Agulhas, following a cold current towards the Indian Ocean. Strange, because it doesn’t benefit the sardines at all. But it’s a bumper buffet for other creatures: dolphins, tuna, seals, sharks, orcas and whales, plus dive-bombing cormorants, gannets and gulls. The result is marine mayhem. The sardines become silvery shape-shifting bait balls, chased down by great gangs of hungry predators and pierced by an avian invasion from above. Fish numbers have plunged in recent decades and the Sardine Run has become less predictable, but it’s still known as one of Earth’s greatest shoals. Activity peaks off Eastern Cape province, with boat trips leaving from towns such as Port St Johns and Gqeberha (formerly Port Elizabeth, handy for Addo Elephant National Park, too). Diving amid this chaos is thrilling, if challenging; snorkellers can launch into the action more quickly. Or, stay on board to watch the feasting frenzy from above.
With their massive bills and bodies, capacious pouches and wide, powerful wings, pelicans look both immensely impressive and distinctly prehistoric. Come spring, around 32,000 of them — mostly great whites, plus a significant scoop of dalmatians, the biggest species — leave their winter hangouts and make for Europe’s largest natural wetland, the Danube Delta. This splurge of rivers, lakes, marshes, forest, sandbars and reedbeds spreads mostly across eastern Romania. It’s a paradise for the pelicans, as well as other birds such as herons, storks and white-tailed eagles. The pelicans begin arriving in March, but May is an ideal time to visit, when colonies are a-bustle, large pods gather for herd-fishing and adults are in full breeding splendour, their great gular pouches beaming bright-orange. June, on the other hand, is good for spying chicks, and July the time to go for sheer numbers. Navigate the delta on boat trips with licensed guides (mandatory for exploring core areas) or stay on a floating hotel for 24/7 avian action.
When to go: July to October
No migration is easy, but the journey of the Pacific Northwest salmon reads like a Greek tragedy. Born in fresh water, they head out to sea, mature for a few years, then navigate back to their natal streams using the earth’s magnetic fields and their own sense of smell. They battle against the flow, leaping rapids, dodging grizzlies and eagles, only to spawn — and then die. It’s a privilege to witness this fatal journey, either from the riverbank, as the fish fling themselves from the froth, or in the water amid the shoals. The town of Campbell River, on Vancouver Island’s east coast, is the self-proclaimed ‘salmon capital of the world’, and the top spot for snorkelling with the chinook, coho, chum, pink and sockeye fighting to return home. Floating in the swift current, you might see hundreds, even thousands, of salmon swim past — and possibly some bears hanging about. From the banks, you can watch salmon leaping two metres into the air, perhaps only to be snatched by those waiting bears. From mid-August to late October, the Homalco First Nation run bear-watching trips to Bute Inlet.
When to go: October to December
The wildebeest in Kenya and Tanzania might grab the headlines, but the world’s biggest mammal migration happens further south. Kasanka National Park is one of Zambia’s smallest and, come October, around 10 million straw-coloured fruit bats overwhelm the remote enclave. By day, they weigh down the trees, wrapped snugly amid  the leaves. But at dusk they take flight, creating a deafening, whirling maelstrom of leathery wings as they seek supper — the bats weigh around 250g and can consume the same in fruit every night. At dawn they return, the maelstrom in reverse.  A good 10-hour drive from the capital of Lusaka, Kasanka National Park is offbeat, but tree hides and viewing platforms ensure the safari-goers who do make the effort get front-row seats. And it isn’t just bats: 114 mammal species have been recorded, from elephant to sitatunga antelope, plus 450 bird species. A trip here combines well with relatively nearby South Luangwa National Park, home to prolific wildlife and pioneering walking safaris.
When to go: June to October
Sea turtles: so cumbersome on land, so graceful underwater. These reptiles swim vast distances across oceans but must return to shore — back to the beach where they were born — to nest. There are seven species worldwide, five have nesting grounds in Costa Rica. Unsurprisingly, given its name is derived from ‘ tortuga ’ — the Spanish word for ‘turtle’ — Tortuguero is a hotspot. This national park on the country’s Caribbean coast is home to the western hemisphere’s largest green turtle rookery, as well as significant populations of leatherbacks and hawksbills.

Nick Seibel, editor and publisher of the Silver City Daily Press, covers top stories each week in the Silver City Report. This week, he updates us on the horse that was infected with New World Screwworm, talks about a recent candidate forum, and more.
Susan Morée: You have an update for us on that poor horse that was infected with New World screw worm. How's the horse doing?
Nick Seibel: Yeah, well, I mean, the horse is recovering. You know, it was according to the veterinarians that treated the horse. The wound on the horse when they discovered it really didn't have the strong odor that's usually associated with that infestation. until they started to clean up the wound and found larvae deeper in the horse's tissue.
Yeah, it was unpleasant, but so far, no new cases reported in the area. Of course, there's an infestation zone, which is a 20 kilometer radius around where the horse was in Mimbres. There's a lot of sort of mystery around that particular infestation, because a lot of folks say, well, did the horse come from somewhere? But as it turns out, the horse had not left that property. Other animals that were on the property hadn't recently traveled on or off of the property. So a lot of mystery around how the fly got there to infect said horse. Generally, the experts say the flies travel at most about a mile or a mile and a half, but they can travel up to 10 miles per day. But not having had any other cases, we don't really know how that came to pass. So whether there's undetected infections that are out there, whether there's infestations in wild animals in the area. At the public meeting, the person from the state said that as far as they knew, the fly could have traveled in the cabin of a truck from somewhere else. You just don't know how that went down. But they are continuing with monitoring. They've got that infestation zone where you're supposed to have permission to transport animals in or out of there. They're also releasing sterile flies throughout the area to try to address the potential for flies out there in the wild and make sure that this doesn't spread any further.
Susan Morée: So if you're driving around in your vehicle and you've got a fly in the vehicle, maybe you want to kill it?
Nick Seibel: I mean, I usually want to do that anyway. One of the things they said is you can't really tell, and it doesn't really look any different from any other fly, to the naked eye.
Susan Morée: I don't think I'm going to get too close to a fly anyway to examine it.
Nick Seibel: This is where having a newspaper subscription really comes in handy because that rolled up newspaper is excellent.
Nick Seibel: That's right.
Susan Morée: I love that you got a little plug in there. And let's talk about the candidate forums for District 39. The election is in November. What was your forum like?
Nick Seibel: Yeah, well, early voting got started, well, got started yesterday, in fact, across New Mexico. Not a lot of contested races on the local level here in Grant County. Most of it was decided in the primary. But there is of course a contested race for Grant County Sheriff, but the Republican candidate there declined to participate, so we won't be able to have one there, which left us with New Mexico House District 39, which is currently held by Republican Luis Terrazas. He's being opposed by Democrat Raul Turrieta, and they squared off in a forum last Friday night sponsored by the Daily Press. That was just one night after they met in a similar forum sponsored by the Grant County Beat, which is an online publication here. In the Thursday night forum, the Beat forum, was confrontational, a little testy at times. And things started out that way in the Friday forum, too. They definitely, you know, the candidates took some hot shots at each other. But it definitely ended on an odd note. I mean, having done a lot of these candidate forums, I can't ever recall anything quite like that. The last audience question that we asked was about, asking each one of them to say something positive about the other's service to the community. And it really got emotional. In fact, the candidates at the conclusion of the question stood up and hugged it out, which was the main photo on our front page on Tuesday at the Daily Press.
Susan Morée: Let's move on to Gila Regional Medical Center. You've got some news for us about that.
Nick Seibel: Yeah, and that's pretty positive news there. Gila Regional, of course, is the county-owned hospital here in Silver City. And they've been named a regional hub in the new state health initiative known as the Healthy Horizons Initiative. They're gonna be coordinating the expenditure of about a little more than $15 million to improve rural healthcare in this part of the state. So Gila Regional is right at the center of that.
Susan Morée: Okay, and where can readers find these stories, Nick?
Nick Seibel: Check us out anytime online at scdailypress.com.

NEW YORK, Oct 7 (Reuters) - The euro tumbled on Wednesday as French bonds came under renewed pressure on fiscal concerns, while the dollar advanced as investors awaited the minutes from the most recent Federal Reserve meeting for clues on the central bank's ‌policy path.
Yields on euro zone bonds rose, with those of more indebted countries spiking more sharply than those of safe havens such as Germany ‌as French fiscal worries dragged on and oil prices came back into focus.
The French 10-year yield surged 14.9 basis points, on track for its biggest daily jump in two weeks, at 4.8959% ​while the German 10-year bond yield edged up 0.8 basis point to 3.489%.
"The case in Europe is that for a while they've operated a bit in a welfare-state type mode, spending a lot of money, not really bringing in a lot of revenue, and it's finally biting them. Considering also the fact that everybody has had to spend more money on energy, the outlook is not good," said Juan Perez, senior director of trading at Monex USA in Washington.
"The focus is on Europe, and ‌it's a very, very negative one."
The euro slumped 0.65% ⁠at $1.1185, closing in on the 17-month lows hit on Monday.
GREENBACK GAINS AHEAD OF FED MINUTES
The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, climbed 0.41% to 102.33 ahead of the minutes from the Fed's September policy meeting, when it ⁠raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 to contend with inflation.
The minutes are expected to show a much broader debate than reflected in the unanimous decision to raise interest rates, with possible implications for the US central bank's next policy steps.
Recent comments from many Fed policymakers have been supportive of more rate hikes, although Federal Reserve ​Bank ​of New York President John Williams and Vice Chair Philip Jefferson last week expressed a ​preference for patience in additional rate increases.
The greenback was also supported ‌by a rise in energy prices, as oil prices advanced on continued Middle East supply risks and a storm heading for oil-producing regions in the US.
"We already kind of understand the dynamic that in a time when it's difficult to access energy resources, the US dollar is going to spike," said Perez.
The chance of a rate hike of at least 25 basis points at the Fed's meeting later this month stands at 21.6%, from about 38% a week ago, according to CME FedWatch, but markets are pricing in an 82.8% chance of a hike at the Fed's December meeting.
FRENCH DEBT UNDER PRESSURE
Bond yields around the world have ‌climbed in recent weeks due to expectations of central bank rate hikes as well as ​concerns about government finances. French debt is under growing pressure as politicians struggle to curb ​the budget deficit ahead of a divisive election in 2027. The calling ​of a snap election in Spain added to the pressure on the euro.
But the euro rebounded on Tuesday after far-right French ‌presidential candidate Marine Le Pen raised her target for spending ​cuts to €140 billion ($158 billion) from €125 billion in ​savings originally planned if she wins power in 2027.
France's economic situation is serious, given the rise in its borrowing costs, but the country does not at this point need help from the European Central Bank, Bank of France head Emmanuel Moulin said.
Sterling weakened 0.45% to $1.3212 against the greenback but ​hit its highest level since June 2025 against the ‌euro.
Against the Japanese yen, the dollar edged up 0.03% to 158.16. The Bank of Japan's new policymaker, Ayano Sato, said in an interview ​with the Kyodo news agency that she supports the idea of raising interest rates in several stages.

articles.title_orig: World Athletics referee and race walking judge Costin's steps to success
articles.title_zh: World Athletics referee and race walking judge Costin's steps to success
articles.content_orig:
Zuzana Costin at the World Athletics U20 Championships Oregon 26 ( © World Athletics Media Academy Lenny Patram Jr. )
Zuzana Costin is a former athlete turned official, currently the only active female technical official in the world to hold both World Athletics Gold Level Referee and Gold Level Race Walking Judge qualifications.
The two-time Olympian, who competed in the 20km race walk at the Athens 2004 and Beijing 2008 Games, most recently served as a race walking judge and referee during the World Athletics U20 Championships Oregon 26. While there, she reflected on her journey in athletics.
You hold both World Athletics Gold Level Referee and Gold Level Race Walking Judge qualifications – currently the only active female technical official in the world to do so. What does this achievement mean to you?
"There are three of us who hold both qualifications but, yes, I am the only female official. It’s quite amazing to have achieved this. I always try to do the best that I can, therefore it’s nice to see that the work I have put in was recognised, and it paid off."
When you first began your journey as a technical official, did you ever imagine you would reach this level?
"No, I didn’t. I got involved in athletics at a very young age. My dad (Jozef Malik) was the Vice President of the federation (Slovak Athletic Federation) for several years and was active as an administrator, coach and also as an official, so I grew up in the world of athletics. Any time he organised any competitions, I was helping out. So it has always been a part of my life and I never thought about it too much at that stage. Achieving this level in officiating in athletics after finishing my racing career gives me a strong sense of accomplishment and satisfaction."
Throughout your career, have there been mentors who helped shape your journey?
"Undeniably, my dad played a big role at the beginning of my journey and he has kept supporting me since.
"After retiring from being an athlete, I started to officiate in Ireland on a regular basis (I had moved there a few years beforehand). I met with support and encouragement to pursue this to an international level. I was very lucky that I was immersed in an environment where people knew what they were doing, not just on a local level but on an international one, too. So, whenever I came across any problems, I had people I could rely on.
"After passing the Silver level exam, I started getting appointments at European competitions and there were always senior technical officials who were happy to share their knowledge and experience with ‘newbies’.
"That was also the case during one of my first big international appointments as a member of the Jury of Appeal at the European Championships in Berlin where Anna Riccardi was our chief. She took me under her wing, gave me confidence and guided me through this new experience.
"During the Covid-19 pandemic, European Athletics began organising online webinars for technical officials, focusing heavily on the practical aspects of officiating. Those webinars were primary led by Chris Cohen and Niels van der Aar and they helped me to become a more knowledgeable and effective official.
"Later, I was selected for the European Athletics mentoring programme for technical delegates and was appointed as a mentee technical delegate for the European Championships in Rome. I was fortunate to have Chris and Niels as my mentors; their guidance provided invaluable insights and allowed me to expand my knowledge even further."
What practical support is most beneficial for upcoming female officials during the early stages of their careers?
"Having someone you can turn to, talk to and learn from is major. Mentorship is something you can’t replace, especially when you are trying to excel.
"After World Athletics changed its educational programme for officials to the current one, it really opened the door for younger people. Originally, the educational programme and exams to become an international official were only in English, which could be a bit of a barrier for people who don’t have a good standard of English. That is still the case for the Gold level. And this could be something that a mentor could help with – dismantling the language barrier. However, for the lower levels, World Athletics has gradually introduced more languages in which its certification courses and exams can be taken. This shift definitely benefits new candidates who don’t have a sufficient command of English."
Since you started your career, have you seen an increase in more female judges, applicants or volunteers for athletics?
"Absolutely. I don’t remember seeing many female officials in the leading positions when I started, and that has definitely changed now. Also, World Athletics’ encouragement to member federations to enter an equal number of female and male candidates for exams has started to pay off. Panels of international officials are now nearly gender balanced.
"I have also seen a growth in the numbers of younger officials, with more opportunities and positions available for them. It’s more achievable and something that one can work towards now."
What kind of advice would you give someone, especially a younger woman, who is interested in following your footsteps or becoming a judge in athletics?
"Now is the right time. Ask your federation about upcoming courses and exams. If you get opportunities to take part in them or you get any appointments, don’t turn them down because you can always learn something. You might not succeed all the time, but you learn from the experience.
"It is also important to believe in yourself and to have someone, or a group of people, that you can get support from.
"It is nice to see new candidates growing in confidence. When they first get started, it’s all very nerve-racking and there’s so much going on all at once – it creates a lot of feelings of fear. But that’s a normal thing to experience. Sometimes all they need is someone in their corner telling them that this is normal, to believe in themselves, and that someone else has confidence in them."
What kind of legacy do you hope to leave – not only through the competitions you’ve officiated, but through the people you’ve inspired?
"I just hope that all the younger officials coming in see that they can do this. That this, as well as whatever else they want to strive for, is achievable regardless of whether they are coming from a country with a strong tradition of international officiating or not. And that the journey of being an international official can start at any age."
