articles.title_orig: Doja Cat’s ‘Tour Ma Vie World Tour’ tests her performer bona fides
articles.title_zh: Doja Cat’s ‘Tour Ma Vie World Tour’ tests her performer bona fides
articles.content_orig:
When an artist abandons the standard fanfare and extravagance of an arena tour, their true performance ability is put to the test. Doja Cat’s “Tour Ma Vie World Tour” demonstrated her showmanship needs no hefty entourage of backup dancers, elaborate sets or choreography.
The tour, which hit Chicago’s United Center on Oct. 3, traverses the R&B artist’s ’80s-infused 2025 album “Vie,” while incorporating older hits like “Need to Know” and “Say So.” Apart from a handful of male backup dancers and occasional pyrotechnics, her tour is largely an understated affair as she commands the audience’s attention almost entirely on her own.
Opening with a hearty brass interlude, Doja Cat began the evening with “Cards,” the first track on “Vie.” Her performance evoked sartorial themes of the ’80s, as she donned pink geometric yoga pants and a bright orange cheetah-patterned coat. Vibrant lighting punctuated the disco-heavy setlist as Doja Cat ventured further into the album, which combines dance-pop and disco.
Her newest album and its accompanying tour are quite a departure for Doja Cat, whose earlier discography is primarily contemporary R&B and rap.
While the show’s runtime focused heavily on “Vie,” Doja Cat gained substantial mileage from older hits like “Need to Know” from her 2021 album “Planet Her” and “Streets” from her 2019 album “Hot Pink,” a testament to her artistic depth.
The concert presents Doja Cat at her most comfortable, highlighting the signature unseriousness that makes her such a compelling performer. At one point, she playfully lit a cigarette before jumping back into song. Later on, she pied an audience member in the face during a tongue-in-cheek interactive skit.
Though there were scattered moments of grandeur, Doja Cat was at her best when she was alone onstage, commanding the audience without flashy costume changes or theatrical gimmicks.
The most memorable track from the evening was unequivocally “Paint The Town Red,” a hit from her 2023 album “Scarlet.” Unaccompanied by background vocals, Doja Cat exerted a larger-than-life stage presence throughout the track, eliciting deafening cheers from the audience.
True to form, Doja Cat concluded the concert on a high note, launching a pyrotechnics show to close out the night and putting her band centerstage for an epic guitar solo. Bouncing between fan favorites like “Tia Tamera” and new songs like “Stranger,” the artist underscored her thematic versatility as a performer.
Though her performance was notably unostentatious, Doja Cat’s “Tour Ma Vie World Tour” proves she is a born performer. With a refined yet metamorphic style, Doja Cat demonstrated she can be as dynamic as she is iconic.

articles.title_zh: FlyDubai Attacker Was Part of Pilot Hiring Spree at Fast-Growing Airline
articles.content_orig:
An Israeli airline El Al aircraft is parked on the tarmac at Ben Gurion Airport near the city of Lod on Friday. Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
TEL AVIV, Israel — An ongoing investigation into last week's midair attack on a FlyDubai plane has found that the co-pilot who tried to take control of the flight intended to crash it into Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport, a person familiar with the matter but not authorized to speak publicly told NPR.
The plane was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv and was intending to land at Ben Gurion midmorning on a busy weekday. The co-pilot attacked the plane's captain midflight with an axe and attempted to take control of the plane.
It is believed that the co-pilot likely acted alone, the source said.
Authorities in the United Arab Emirates — which is leading the main investigation into the incident, with help from Israeli officials — and in Israel have deemed the attack an attempted terrorist attack, although the motive is still being investigated.
The commercial flight had 172 people on board, according to the airline, the majority of whom were Israeli. All passengers and crew were safe and accounted for after the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. They were flown to Tel Aviv late Wednesday.
Investigators said that the co-pilot carried out the attack with what's called a crash axe — a lightweight emergency tool stored in the cockpit to break through panels or jammed doors in the event of a crash.
The aviation tracking site Flightradar24 said data shows at one point the plane descended more than 14,000 feet, or nearly 3 miles, in under 30 seconds — way faster than normal.
The pilot was able to open the cockpit door during the attack, and passengers rushed in and subdued the attacker, while another pilot who happened to be on board helped land the plane, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who spoke to the injured pilot as he was recovering in the hospital.
Both the pilot and the co-pilot are alive and have been transferred to the UAE for questioning.
The co-pilot is from Oman, according to Israeli officials. Omani and Emirati officials have not confirmed that publicly.
The detail of his nationality is raising questions in Israel about how he was allowed to fly a plane heading to Ben Gurion, as Israel does not allow pilots from countries it doesn't have diplomatic relations with to fly in its airspace. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Fox & Friends that Israel checks the background of pilots flying routes into the country, and that the attacker must have gotten through a "loophole."
Officials from Israel's Ministry of Transportation and security services have traded accusations over the lack of oversight and vetting of the pilot. Meanwhile, several of Netanyahu's political opponents have said the security breach is a failure on the prime minister's part and have called for a larger investigation.
Netanyahu announced late Sunday that there will be a formal examination into the security situation around "foreign civil aviation into Israel," but did not provide further details.
National elections in Israel — which will determine whether or not Netanyahu will remain prime minister — are just weeks away. It's the first such national election since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which sparked the war in Gaza.
Polls in Israel show that the race is tight, and analysts say the FlyDubai attack would likely not change Israelis' attitudes on how they will vote.
Netanyahu has been campaigning largely on the idea that he alone can protect Israelis from the external threats that Israel faces, while his opponents have pointed to what they see as major security failures under his leadership — including the Oct. 7 attack.

articles.title_zh: Germany news: Far-right AfD gets first house speaker in a German state parliament
articles.content_orig:
This blog has now closed. Read below for a look at the latest news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 6, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Germany plans to buy four more Meko A-200 frigates from TKMS for about €5.6 million   ($6.3 billion), the Reuters news agency reported on Tuesday, citing a Finance Ministry document.
The country's parliamentary budget committee is expected to approve the purchase on Thursday, with the construction due to be finalized by 2035, as per Finance Ministry documents seen by Reuters.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius had cancelled a rival F126  frigate project with Dutch company Damen , over delays and cost overruns.
Germany’s far-right AfD party took a significant step toward exercising political power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
One month after winning 44% of the regional vote, the party secured the presidency of the state parliament, with Tobias Rausch elected as speaker of the house.
What does this moment mean for Germany? DW reports from Magdeburg.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Parliamentarians in Saxony-Anhalt have also voted for AfD politician Hans-Thomas Tillschneider to be one of the deputy speakers in the chamber.
This follows Tobias Rausch of the right-wing populist AfD being voted into the speaker's role earlier on Tuesday.
Tillschneider received 44 votes in favor in Tuesday's session, while 38 parliamentarians opposed his appointment. Nobody abstained from the vote, which was by secret ballot. The AfD has 39 seats in the chamber.
Lawmakers decided to elect three deputy speakers in total, with elections for the others expected to follow later.
Tillschneider, aged 48, is the deputy chair of the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt parliamentary group. He's an AfD veteran, having joined the party in 2013 soon after it was founded.
Tillschneider is a member of the identitarian movement, and was a member of the two AfD fringe groups — the so-called Flügel (wing) and its "Patriotic Platform" — that have since been formally disbanded. He also had close ties to the Pegida and Legida groups that organized anti-migrant protests in eastern Germany.
As well as his strong views on Islam and migration, Tillschneider is also known for his ties to Vladimir Putin's Russia. He was one of three AfD parliamentarians to visit Russia in September 2022, barely six months after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine , in a visit that AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel rapidly disowned as a "private trip" and "not productive."
Since 2023, Tillschneider has written a monthly column for the Vedomosti newspaper in Russia. He attended the 73rd birthday celebrations for Putin at the Russian Embassy in Berlin last October.
The outgoing premier of Saxony-Anhalt says he can't explain where an additional four votes backing the AfD's Tobias Rausch as the state's new parliamentary speaker came from.
In a first for the far-right party, 35-year-old Rausch was elected to the post on Tuesday with the help of the populist BSW party (see entry below).
The Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group leadership had recommended that its 15 lawmakers in the state parliament abstain from voting.
But CDU regional leader and current state Premier Sven Schulze said it had become clear by this morning that not all the party's lawmakers planned to do so.
Some indicated that they planned to vote "no," Schulze said in comments to the German press agency DPA. "But none of us said we would vote 'yes,'" he added. "Not a single one."
Rausch was elected with 48 votes in favor and 29 against from 82 eligible votes in the secret ballot. There were five abstentions.
The AfD holds 39 seats in the parliament and the BSW five, meaning Rausch also got backing from members of other parties besides the AfD and BSW.
The center-left Social Democrats demanded answers, with the party's general secretary, Tim Klüssendorf, calling for the CDU to "immediately clarify who from within its ranks may have considered this disastrous decision to be right."
Klüssendorf also criticized the BSW for supporting Rausch's election.
"The BSW has made a conscious decision to elect, for the first time since 1945, a politician from a far-right party to the leadership of a German parliament," Klüssendorf told the Rheinische Post newspaper.
In addition to the CDU, the Social Democrats and the BSW, the Left party and the Greens are also represented in the state's parliament. Except for the BSW, the other parties have refused to work with the AfD, but some combination of them cast a secret vote for Rausch.
The Volksbank Köln Bonn in western Germany has agreed to part ways with a board member, Jürgen Neutgens, after a scandal over a loan he authorized to Cologne 's large brothel, Pascha.
It made the announcement on Tuesday, several months after placing Neutgens on leave and commissioning an independent law firm to investigate the transaction for potential wrongdoing.
"The investigation ... found no indications of financial irregularities or actions contravening obligations in the loan processes or the business relationship," the bank said in a press release . "Nevertheless the past weeks have weighed considerably on everyone involved."
Against this backdrop, the bank said the parties involved had mutually concluded that "a trusting and candid cooperation for the future can no longer be continued on the appropriate foundation."
It said both sides had agreed to confidentiality on the further details and terms, and thanked Neutgens for his service and wished him well for the future.
The loan was issued amid the restrictions of the COVID pandemic, which took a severe toll on the sex industry in Germany and led to the Pascha brothel in Cologne filing for insolvency and then changing ownership .
A family from China, or more specifically the autonomous casino-rich region of Macao, bought the business. But they needed a bridging loan of around €5 million (roughly $5.6 million at today's exchange rates) to cover part of the purchase price when their funds were held up in Hong Kong.
A typical German Christmas speciality intended as a gift for Pope Leo XIV was driven to Rome in an official vehicle from the state of Saxony after it was deemed unsuitable for air transport, officials revealed on Tuesday.
The 4-kilogram (8.8-pound) cake, a so-called stollen, which was made in the Ore Mountains in eastern Germany, was taken by Saxon Premier Michael Kretschmer to the Vatican for a private audience at the end of September.
The cake was reportedly too large to be taken into the cabin and too fragile to be placed in the aircraft hold, the officials said.
No information was provided on the cost by the officials at the Saxon State Chancellery.
The vehicle also transported other presents and documents.
The leader of the Green parliamentary party in Saxony-Anhalt , Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, has vowed to defend democracy following the election of a member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) , Tobias Rausch, as parliamentary speaker.
The election of the member of a confirmed right-wing extremist, anti-constitutional party as house speaker meant that a "border" had been crossed, she said.
"We will not allow ourselves to be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights here or those of the people in this state are to be curtailed," she added.
Earlier in her address, she said that if the AfD were to take power in the state, her party would "speak out if people were denigrated because of their origins, beliefs or lifestyle."
Sziborra-Seidlitz said Saxony-Anhalt could not afford for "exclusion to become the political brand of this parliament and our state."
The AfD emerged from September elections as the strongest single force in parliament but has so far failed to find parties willing to enter into a coalition with it.

By Charity L. Cohen / 10/06/2026 Alumni , College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences
EAST GREENSBORO, N.C. (Oct. 6, 2026) – Forever a North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University Aggie and now a Hillman College Falcon, former Mister A&T Joshua Suiter ‘22 is starring in the Netflix reboot of the 1980s and 1990s hit sitcom “A Different World.”
The series, which debuted at No. 1 on Netflix in the U.S., has already been renewed for a second season. It builds on the cultural impact of the original series, which helped shape national perceptions of historically Black college and university (HBCU) life and inspired generations of students.
Following a new generation of students at the iconic fictional HBCU, Hillman College, the sequel explores the lives of today’s students while examining the legacy of those who came before them. The series’ writing team includes Ashley Laverne Jackson, daughter of late civil rights leader the Rev. Jesse Jackson ‘64.
Suiter portrays Andre, a fellow Hillman student alongside Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), daughter of original characters Whitley (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison). As Deborah begins her journey at Hillman, she works to establish her own identity beyond her parents’ legacy while experiencing the highs and challenges of campus life.
“Seeing all the love for Andre really hit home,” Suiter said. “He’s one of my favorite characters thus far, and we created him from scratch, so to know that the hard work is being received and folks want more encourages me to keep going.”
Suiter discovered his calling for acting and musical theater at 7, quickly realizing that hours spent studying lines and practicing techniques felt like minutes. That passion led him to N.C. A&T, where he earned a B.F.A. in professional theatre from the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences.
While at A&T, Suiter built a strong foundation in the performing arts, gaining experience both on stage and behind the scenes. One of his notable performances was in “Ain’t Misbehavin’” during the university’s first Town & Gown Gala in 2019, where he first met Guy, who reprises her role as Whitley in the reboot.
In addition to acting, Suiter worked as a theater technician and developed skills in the marketing and business aspects of performance and the entertainment industry. This versatility helped propel him into his professional career.
“I came in as a creative, but what A&T did between Alpha Phi Alpha, the classes, talking business with professors and serving as Mister A&T sharpened me on the business side,” said Suiter. “It sharpened my networking skills while showing me how to be authentic to who I am.”
As a talented and emerging actor who most recently appeared in the Hulu series “All’s Fair,” performing alongside prominent Hollywood actors, starring in “A Different World” represents a full-circle moment for Suiter as an HBCU alumnus, bringing him into a reimagined version of a series he grew up watching.
“When you talk about an HBCU experience, I’m putting mine up there with the best of them,” he said. “I have so many experiences to pull from with the run of this show, with the character Andre. Hillman even has a heartbeat of its own, so it’s been fun exploring what that feels like as a student there, while still carrying that Aggie Pride in my heart.”

Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers are investigating turbulent planetary systems in which worlds violently collide. This investigation could shed light on the hypothetical collision between Earth and a Mars-sized planetary body called Theia , which is thought to have spilled matter around our planet that coalesced to forge the moon billions of years ago.
Young planetary systems are notoriously violent, featuring young stars surrounded by disks of gas and dust called protoplanetary disks. Within these disks, small bodies called planetesimals collide and stick together to begin the process of forming planets. However, NASA's now-retired Spitzer Space Telescope discovered that there is a class of protoplanetary disks that are even more violent than usual, so-called extreme debris disks. These systems contain unusually large amounts of warm dust close to the young star, in the region similar to that occupied by rocky planets in the solar system.
Investigating extreme debris disks is challenging, partially because they are so rare. Scientists estimate that such systems exist around just 1% of stars. It is suspected that our sun was one of these rare stars.
A team of scientists set about investigating 21 extreme debris disks with the incredible observing power of the JWST . This included follow-ups on four of the five of these environments from Spitzer's archival data and 16 from the JWST, with 12 newly observed disks
"This is the first time we have gathered enough systems to truly understand this subclass that we call extreme debris disks," team leader Kate Su of the Space Science Institute in Boulder, Colorado, said in a statement . "Before the JWST, we had limited information. We knew that they are weird and very different from the typical cold debris disks that we know, like Vega and Fomalhaut .
"Now that we have more data, we can pin down what these disks represent for planet formation and evolution."
The researchers discovered that there are three properties common to extreme debris disks. They contain smaller dust grains than those found in "classic" protoplanetary disks, a high concentration of warm dust, and irregular variations in brightness.
The next step was to discover what was driving these features. To do this, the team investigated the minerals that composed the disks they investigated, finding they could be categorized as silica-rich or silica-poor.
This told the scientists which type of collisions were occurring in those disks and producing impact debris. These collisions may also help account for its variability in brightness seen in these systems.
"To just see their mid-infrared emission and beautiful spectral features with the JWST, which allowed us to identify their compositions, was the most exciting thing for me," team member Agnes Kospal of Konkoly Observatory in Budapest, Hungary, said. "We have no other way to study these planetary embryos directly because they are too small."
The researchers think that silica-rich disks are produced by high-energy impacts of Mars-sized objects, in which most of the material is vaporized. Silica-poor disks are created by less energetic events from roughly moon-sized bodies grazing each other.
From their sample, around one-third of extreme debris disks are silica-rich disks. These were found only around stars younger than 300 million years. Silica-poor disks, on the other hand, were found around stars with a broad range of ages. They also often show greater brightness variability than silica-rich disks. The researchers propose that this variability in brightness is caused by the rapid evolution of fresh debris through further impacts and changes in the orbits of the system's occupants.
The findings can now be applied to the solar system to build a better picture of its 4.6-billion-year evolution. Simulations recreating the earliest era of the solar system show that terrestrial planets, such as Earth, should form within the first few hundred million years.
That lines up with the ages of observed silica-rich extreme debris disks and also aligns with the estimated formation of the Earth and the moon around 100 million years after the sun formed.
The solar system likely also went through a silica-poor extreme disk phase during a period called the Late Heavy Bombardment . It is during this period that scientists think collisions may have caused the solar system's gas giants to migrate from close to the sun to the positions they now occupy.
"How rocky planets formed and giant planets evolved are part of the broader story of the solar system’s formation. It’s all one story," said Su. "Our work on extreme debris disks helps us bring together the big picture of what we currently understand."
The team's research was published on Thursday (Oct. 1) in The Astrophysical Journal .
